pos: v. (cut short; of days curtailed in judgment, of the LORD's hand which is not shortened, and of the tribulation shortened for the elect's sake)
etymology: From short — Old English sceort — with the verbal ending. The Hebrew is qatsar, to reap or cut off, and so to shorten; the Greek at Matthew 24:22 is koloboo, to amputate or cut off a limb.
biblical_def: Three distinct uses, and each carries weight. Of a life cut off: “The days of his youth hast thou shortened: thou hast covered him with shame” (Psalm 89:45), and as a proverb, “The fear of the LORD prolongeth days: but the years of the wicked shall be shortened” (Proverbs 10:27). Of God's power, in the great rhetorical question and its answer: “Is my hand shortened at all, that it cannot redeem?” (Isaiah 50:2), and “Behold, the LORD'S hand is not shortened, that it cannot save; neither his ear heavy, that it cannot hear” (Isaiah 59:1). The idiom pictures an arm too short to reach, and Isaiah denies it absolutely — the following clause of chapter 59 names what actually separates: but your iniquities have separated between you and your God. Third, and most striking, of the tribulation: “except those days should be shortened, there should no flesh be saved: but for the elect's sake those days shall be shortened” (Matthew 24:22). Mark adds who does the shortening and for whom: the Lord shortened them, for the elect's sake, whom he hath chosen (Mark 13:20). The doctrine of election is stated in the middle of the darkest prophecy in the Gospels, and it is stated as the reason anyone survives.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines shorten as to make short in measure or time, to abridge, to lessen — and figuratively to restrain or hinder.
webster_full: SHORTENED, pp. Made shorter; abridged; contracted.
SHORTEN, v.t. To make short in measure, extent or time; as, to shorten distance.
2. To abridge; to lessen; as, to shorten labor or work.
3. To confine; to restrain. Shorten my days thou canst not.
4. To lop; to cut off. Is the Lord's hand shortened? Num. 11.
scriptures: Isaiah 59:1
Behold, the LORD'S hand is not shortened, that it cannot save; neither his ear heavy, that it cannot hear:
Isaiah 50:2

Wherefore, when I came, was there no man? when I called, was there none to answer? Is my hand shortened at all, that it cannot redeem? or have I no power to deliver? behold, at my rebuke I dry up the sea, I make the rivers a wilderness: their fish stinketh, because there is no water, and dieth for thirst.
Matthew 24:22
And except those days should be shortened, there should no flesh be saved: but for the elect's sake those days shall be shortened.
Mark 13:20
And except that the Lord had shortened those days, no flesh should be saved: but for the elect's sake, whom he hath chosen, he hath shortened the days.
corruption_summary: Unanswered prayer is explained by a God who cannot rather than a God who will not, and Isaiah 59:1 forecloses that explanation.
corruption_paragraphs: When prayer goes unanswered the two comfortable explanations are that God was unable and that God is indifferent. Isaiah 59:1 blocks both, and then verse 2 supplies the actual answer: your iniquities have separated between you and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you. That is a harder word than either evasion and it is the merciful one, because sin can be confessed and the arm that is not shortened can still reach. Open theism's account — a God genuinely limited in knowledge and therefore in power to guarantee outcomes — is precisely the shortened hand Isaiah denies, and it purchases an explanation for suffering at the cost of the only God who can end it.

Matthew 24:22 is where election appears in the Olivet discourse, and it is often read past. The logic is stark: the days are so severe that no flesh would survive them; they are cut short; the reason given is the elect. Not the deserving, not the majority, not the general goodness of humanity — the elect, and Mark adds whom he hath chosen. The doctrine that modern readers find cold is set here as the reason the world is not destroyed, which is how Scripture generally uses it. Election in the Bible is never an abstract decree; it is the ground of preservation, of assurance, and here of the shortening of the worst days there will ever be.
roots_summary: Hebrew qatsar, to cut off, shorten — Isaiah 50:2, 59:1, Proverbs 10:27; Greek koloboo, to amputate — Matthew 24:22, Mark 13:20; eklektos, elect — the reason given.
roots_lines: Hebrew qatsar — to reap, cut off, be short; Isaiah 59:1 of the hand that is not shortened.
Hebrew yad — the hand or arm; the idiom is of a reach too short to save.
Greek koloboo — to cut off, amputate; Matthew 24:22 and Mark 13:20, of the days.
Greek eklektos — chosen, elect; the stated reason the days are cut short.
Greek sarx — flesh; “there should no flesh be saved.”
usage: “The LORD'S hand is not shortened” — and the next verse names what does separate.
“For the elect's sake those days shall be shortened” — election as the ground of survival.
“The years of the wicked shall be shortened” — the proverb's plain arithmetic.

pos: v. (kept back; the word twice spoken over Abraham on Moriah, and the word Paul reverses at Calvary)
etymology: From withhold — Old English with-, against or back, and healdan, to hold. The Hebrew at Genesis 22:12 is chasak, to restrain, spare, or keep back; the Greek Paul uses at Romans 8:32 is pheidomai, to spare.
biblical_def: The word carries the whole weight of Genesis 22. Twice on Moriah the angel of the LORD names the same thing: “now I know that thou fearest God, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son from me” (Genesis 22:12), and in the oath that follows, “By myself have I sworn, saith the LORD, for because thou hast done this thing, and hast not withheld thy son, thine only son” (Genesis 22:16). The repetition marks it as the hinge of the chapter. Elsewhere the same verb describes God restraining a man from sin — “I also withheld thee from sinning against me” (Genesis 20:6), said to Abimelech, a striking testimony to God's preventing grace toward a pagan king — and God withholding a blessing: “Am I in God's stead, who hath withheld from thee the fruit of the womb?” (Genesis 30:2). Paul takes the Moriah language and turns it toward the Father: “He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). Abraham did not withhold and the knife was stopped; God did not spare, and it was not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines withhold as to hold back, to restrain, to keep from action — and also to retain, to keep back what belongs to another.
webster_full: WITHHELD, pp. of withhold. Held back; kept from action.
WITHHOLD, v.t. To hold back; to restrain; to keep from action.
Withhold, O Lord, thy hand.
2. To retain; to keep back; not to grant.
3. To keep; not to give. Withhold not good from them to whom it is due. Prov. 3.
scriptures: Genesis 22:12
And he said, Lay not thine hand upon the lad, neither do thou any thing unto him: for now I know that thou fearest God, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son from me.
Genesis 22:16
And said, By myself have I sworn, saith the LORD, for because thou hast done this thing, and hast not withheld thy son, thine only son:
Genesis 20:6
And God said unto him in a dream, Yea, I know that thou didst this in the integrity of thy heart; for I also withheld thee from sinning against me: therefore suffered I thee not to touch her.
Romans 8:32
He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things?
corruption_summary: Genesis 22 is condemned as divine child-endangerment, and read that way it loses both the substitution at its centre and the Father it prefigures.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern objection to Genesis 22 is that a God who commands such a thing is a monster, and the chapter is either rejected or reduced to a polemic against the child sacrifice of the surrounding nations. The chapter itself supplies the answers. God stopped the knife, and He stopped it before it fell, so that the one thing the narrative absolutely refuses is the death of Isaac. A ram was provided in the thicket and offered in the stead of his son — substitution stated in as many words. And Abraham had told the young men that he and the lad would come again, and told Isaac that God would provide Himself a lamb; Hebrews says he accounted that God was able to raise him up.

The deepest answer is Paul's. Romans 8:32 deliberately echoes the Septuagint of Genesis 22 — he that spared not his own Son — and the point of the echo is that what Abraham was not required to complete, God completed. On Moriah a father was stopped; at Calvary no voice called from heaven, no ram was in the thicket, and the Son cried why hast thou forsaken me. Everyone who reads Genesis 22 and feels its horror has understood something true; the horror is the measure of what the Father did not withhold. And Paul's argument runs from the greater to the lesser: having given the Son, He will not now be stingy with anything else.
roots_summary: Hebrew chasak, to restrain, spare, keep back — Genesis 22:12, 22:16, 20:6; yachid, only one, only-begotten — the word for Isaac; Greek pheidomai, to spare — Romans 8:32.
roots_lines: Hebrew chasak — to withhold, restrain, spare; the key verb of Genesis 22, used twice.
Hebrew yachid — only, only-begotten; “thy son, thine only son,” the Septuagint's agapetos.
Hebrew tachath — in the stead of; Genesis 22:13, the ram offered in Isaac's place.
Greek pheidomai — to spare; Romans 8:32, the deliberate echo of the Genesis language.
Greek paradidomi — to deliver up; the verb of the Father giving the Son.
usage: “Thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son” — said twice, the hinge of Moriah.
“I also withheld thee from sinning against me” — preventing grace toward a pagan king.
“He that spared not his own Son” — what Abraham was not required to finish.

pos: a. (disposed to show favour; the word of the psalmist's hardest question and of the answer his own memory supplies)
etymology: From Latin favorabilis, from favere, to be kind toward. The Hebrew at Psalm 77:7 is ratsah, to be pleased with or accept — the same verb used of a sacrifice being accepted; at Psalm 85:1 it is the same root.
biblical_def: Asaph asks the question every afflicted believer eventually asks: “Will the Lord cast off for ever? and will he be favourable no more?” (Psalm 77:7). The psalm continues with four more questions of the same kind — is His mercy clean gone for ever, doth His promise fail, hath God forgotten to be gracious, hath He in anger shut up His tender mercies — and then turns on a decision: I will remember the years of the right hand of the most High. Asaph does not receive new information. He goes back over what God has already done, chiefly the exodus, and the psalm ends with the LORD leading His people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron. The Korahite psalm supplies exactly that kind of memory as its opening: “LORD, thou hast been favourable unto thy land: thou hast brought back the captivity of Jacob” (Psalm 85:1). Elihu states the ground on which a man may look for it: “He shall pray unto God, and he will be favourable unto him: and he shall see his face with joy” (Job 33:26). The Hebrew ratsah is sacrificial — to be accepted — so the question is finally whether God will receive the worshipper.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines favourable as kind, propitious, conducive to, and affording advantage or convenience.
webster_full: FAVORABLE, a. Kind; propitious; friendly; affectionate.
Lord, thou hast been favorable to thy land. Ps. 85.
2. Palliative; tender; averse to censure.
3. Conducive to; contributing to; tending to promote.
4. Convenient; advantageous; affording means to a desirable end; as, a favorable position.
scriptures: Psalm 77:7
Will the Lord cast off for ever? and will he be favourable no more?
Psalm 85:1
To the chief Musician, A Psalm for the sons of Korah. LORD, thou hast been favourable unto thy land: thou hast brought back the captivity of Jacob.
He shall pray unto God, and he will be favourable unto him: and he shall see his face with joy: for he will render unto man his righteousness.
Judges 21:22

And it shall be, when their fathers or their brethren come unto us to complain, that we will say unto them, Be favourable unto them for our sakes: because we reserved not to each man his wife in the war: for ye did not give unto them at this time, that ye should be guilty.
corruption_summary: God's favour is measured by circumstance, so that prosperity is read as approval and affliction as displeasure — the error of Job's friends, now marketed.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity teaching makes God's favour legible in a bank balance, and the instinct behind it is older than any preacher: Job's friends held the same doctrine and Job's comforters argued it for thirty chapters. Psalm 77 is the standing refutation, because Asaph is a believer in real darkness who cannot see one favourable circumstance and who is not told that his reading of his circumstances is wrong. He is not given an explanation at all. What he does is go back to what God has done in history — the redemption out of Egypt, the sea, the way through great waters where His footsteps were not known — and reason from settled fact rather than from present feeling.

The method matters more than any argument. Asaph says this is my infirmity about his own despairing questions, and then deliberately turns his memory to God's past acts. That is the discipline the Psalms teach: not the denial of what one feels, which they never do, but the refusal to let feeling be the final witness. For the Christian the memory is fuller than Asaph's. The question will he be favourable no more is answered at the cross, where the acceptance was purchased, and the Hebrew ratsah — the sacrificial word for an offering received — is exactly the right word for it.
roots_summary: Hebrew ratsah, to be pleased with, to accept — Psalm 77:7, 85:1, Job 33:26; ratson, favour or acceptance; chanan, to be gracious — the companion idea.
roots_lines: Hebrew ratsah — to be pleased with, accept favourably; used of a sacrifice being received.
Hebrew ratson — goodwill, acceptance; the noun of the same root, as in “acceptable year of the LORD.”
Hebrew chanan — to be gracious, show favour; Psalm 77:9, “forgotten to be gracious.”
Hebrew zakar — to remember; Psalm 77:11, the turn of the whole psalm.
Latin favere, to be kind toward — the source of the English word.
usage: “Will he be favourable no more?” — the question, and no answer given but memory.
“I will remember the years of the right hand of the most High” — Asaph's method.
Ratsah is the sacrificial word: whether the worshipper is accepted.

pos: v. (past participle of begin; of a plague already spreading, of a conquest God announces as started, and of the good work God will perform)
etymology: From Old English beginnan, to begin. The Hebrew at Deuteronomy 2:31 is chalal, to begin or make a start; the Greek at Philippians 1:6 is enarchomai, to begin in, set against epiteleo, to complete or bring to an end.
biblical_def: Three uses show the range. Of a judgment already in motion, and of an intercession made in haste: “Take a censer, and put fire therein from off the altar, and put on incense, and go quickly unto the congregation, and make an atonement for them: for there is wrath gone out from the LORD; the plague is begun” (Numbers 16:46). Aaron ran into the midst of the congregation and stood between the dead and the living, and the plague was stayed — one of the clearest pictures of priestly mediation in the Pentateuch. Of a work God announces as already underway: “Behold, I have begun to give Sihon and his land before thee: begin to possess, that thou mayest inherit his land” (Deuteronomy 2:31). God's beginning is the ground of Israel's beginning, and the order is never reversed. Moses uses the same word in prayer: “thou hast begun to shew thy servant thy greatness, and thy mighty hand” (Deuteronomy 3:24). Paul gives the word its greatest use: “Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6) — the doctrine of perseverance stated as an inference from who started the work.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives begun as the participle of begin, and defines begin as to have an original or first existence, to take rise, to commence.
webster_full: BEGUN, pp. of begin. Commenced; originated.
BEGIN, v.i. To have an original or first existence; to take rise; to commence.
As, the Christian era began in the fourth year of the four hundred and ninety-fourth Olympiad.
2. To do the first act; to enter upon something new.
BEGINNING, n. The first cause; origin. I am the beginning and the ending. Rev. 1.
scriptures: Philippians 1:6
Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:
Deuteronomy 2:31
And the LORD said unto me, Behold, I have begun to give Sihon and his land before thee: begin to possess, that thou mayest inherit his land.
Deuteronomy 3:24
O Lord GOD, thou hast begun to shew thy servant thy greatness, and thy mighty hand: for what God is there in heaven or in earth, that can do according to thy works, and according to thy might?
Numbers 16:46

And Moses said unto Aaron, Take a censer, and put fire therein from off the altar, and put on incense, and go quickly unto the congregation, and make an atonement for them: for there is wrath gone out from the LORD; the plague is begun.
corruption_summary: Philippians 1:6 is applied to any personal ambition, when Paul's confidence rests entirely on the identity of the one who began the work.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is printed on graduation cards and applied to careers, houses, and diets, with the sense that whatever a person has started God will help them finish. Paul's grammar will not carry it. The subject of both verbs is God: he which hath begun and will perform. The Philippians are the field, not the farmer, and Paul's confidence is not in their persistence but in the fact that the work was never theirs to start. This is the doctrine of perseverance of the saints in one sentence, and it is inseparable from effectual calling — the same God who began it is the one who guarantees the completion, and the guarantee is dated: until the day of Jesus Christ.

The Old Testament uses guard the doctrine from becoming passive. God says I have begun to give Sihon, and in the same breath says begin to possess. The divine beginning does not replace the human action; it commands and enables it, which is exactly Paul's work out your own salvation with fear and trembling: for it is God which worketh in you two chapters later in the same epistle. Numbers 16:46 shows the urgency the doctrine permits: the plague is begun, and Aaron runs. Confidence in God's finishing has never in Scripture produced a man standing still.
roots_summary: Hebrew chalal, to begin — Deuteronomy 2:31, 3:24; Greek enarchomai, to begin in — Philippians 1:6; epiteleo, to complete — the paired verb.
roots_lines: Hebrew chalal — to begin, make a start; Deuteronomy 2:31, of God beginning to give Sihon.
Greek enarchomai — to begin in or among; Philippians 1:6 and Galatians 3:3.
Greek epiteleo — to complete, bring to an end; the answering verb, rendered perform.
Greek peitho — to be persuaded, confident; the participle behind “being confident.”
Hebrew magephah — a plague or stroke; Numbers 16:46, already begun when Aaron ran.
usage: “He which hath begun a good work in you will perform it” — both verbs have God as subject.
“I have begun to give Sihon… begin to possess” — the divine start commands the human one.
“The plague is begun” — and Aaron ran between the dead and the living.

pos: v. (to grow less; the Baptist's own account of his ministry set against Christ's, and a mercy promised over a man's cattle)
etymology: From Latin decrescere, to grow less, from de- and crescere, to grow. The Greek at John 3:30 is elattoo, to make less; the Hebrew at Psalm 107:38 is maat, to become small or few.
biblical_def: The great occurrence is five words long: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). John the Baptist's disciples had come to him troubled that the crowds were going to Jesus, and this was his answer. He had already given the figure that explains it: “He that hath the bride is the bridegroom: but the friend of the bridegroom, which standeth and heareth him, rejoiceth greatly because of the bridegroom's voice: this my joy therefore is fulfilled” (John 3:29). The friend of the bridegroom arranged the wedding and then stepped out of it; his whole office was to bring the two together, and his gladness came from hearing the bridegroom's voice, not from being heard himself. The must in verse 30 is a divine necessity, not a resolution John made — it was appointed that he should diminish. The only other occurrence is a quiet mercy in the psalm of the redeemed: God “blesseth them also, so that they are multiplied greatly; and suffereth not their cattle to decrease” (Psalm 107:38). The same God who appoints a man's decrease keeps a poor man's herd from dwindling.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines decrease as to become less, to be diminished gradually in extent, bulk, quantity, or amount.
webster_full: DECREASE, v.i. To become less; to be diminished gradually, in extent, bulk, quantity, or amount, or in strength, quality or excellence.
He must increase, but I must decrease. John 3.
DECREASE, v.t. To lessen; to make smaller in dimensions, amount, quality or excellence.
DECREASE, n. A becoming less; gradual diminution; decay.
2. The wane of the moon; the wane or decline of the moon's illuminated part.
scriptures: John 3:30
He must increase, but I must decrease.
John 3:29
He that hath the bride is the bridegroom: but the friend of the bridegroom, which standeth and heareth him, rejoiceth greatly because of the bridegroom's voice: this my joy therefore is fulfilled.
Psalm 107:38
He blesseth them also, so that they are multiplied greatly; and suffereth not their cattle to decrease.
John 3:27
John answered and said, A man can receive nothing, except it be given him from heaven.
corruption_summary: John 3:30 is used as a slogan for self-deprecation, when it is a statement about the structure of an office and the joy proper to it.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse has been reduced to a sentiment about personal humility, roughly equivalent to thinking less of oneself. John says something more definite and more freeing. He states the fact of an office: he is the friend of the bridegroom, not the bridegroom, and a wedding does not go wrong when the best man leaves the couple alone — that is the wedding working. He also grounds the whole thing in a doctrine two verses earlier: a man can receive nothing, except it be given him from heaven. His decrease is not modesty about a ministry he owned; it is accuracy about a ministry he had been lent.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the joy attached. John does not say I must decrease with resignation; he says this my joy therefore is fulfilled, and the fulfilment is in hearing the bridegroom's voice. A ministry, a parent, a teacher, or an older believer whose usefulness is visibly being succeeded by someone else can grieve the loss or can hear the voice. Our Lord's verdict on the man who spoke this sentence is that among them born of women there had not risen a greater. He decreased on schedule and lost nothing.
roots_summary: Greek elattoo, to make or become less — John 3:30; auxano, to increase — the paired verb; dei, it is necessary — the divine must; Hebrew maat, to diminish — Psalm 107:38.
roots_lines: Greek elattoo — to make less, decrease; John 3:30, and Hebrews 2:7 of Christ made lower than the angels.
Greek auxano — to grow, increase; the paired verb of the same verse.
Greek dei — it is necessary, it must be; a divine appointment, not a personal resolve.
Greek philos tou numphiou — the friend of the bridegroom; the office John claims.
Hebrew maat — to be or become few; Psalm 107:38, of cattle not suffered to decrease.
usage: “He must increase, but I must decrease” — a divine must, not a resolution.
“The friend of the bridegroom… rejoiceth greatly” — the joy of the office fulfilled.
“A man can receive nothing, except it be given him from heaven” — the ground of it all.

pos: v. (to make rich; the prize offered for killing Goliath, the trade by which Tyre enriched kings, and God's enriching of the saints unto liberality)
etymology: From Old French enrichir, from en- and riche, rich — of Germanic origin. The Hebrew at 1 Samuel 17:25 is ashar, to be or make rich; the Greek at 2 Corinthians 9:11 is ploutizo, to make wealthy.
biblical_def: Three enrichings, and they sort the doctrine neatly. The first is the wage offered for courage: “the man who killeth him, the king will enrich him with great riches, and will give him his daughter, and make his father's house free in Israel” (1 Samuel 17:25). David heard the offer, asked about it twice, and then went down to the brook and chose five stones — and the reason he gave the giant was not the reward but that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel. The second is commercial and ends in ruin: of Tyre, “thou didst enrich the kings of the earth with the multitude of thy riches and of thy merchandise” (Ezekiel 27:33), a sentence that stands in the middle of a lament for her sinking. The third is Paul's and it names the purpose: “Being enriched in every thing to all bountifulness, which causeth through us thanksgiving to God” (2 Corinthians 9:11). The Greek construction is purposive — enriched unto liberality. God does not make His people rich and then hope they will give; He enriches them for the giving, and the end of the transaction is thanksgiving offered to God by those who received.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines enrich as to make rich in money or property, to fertilize, and figuratively to supply with any thing splendid or valuable.
webster_full: ENRICH, v.t. To make rich, wealthy or opulent; to increase the possessions of.
The king will enrich him with great riches. 1 Sam. 17.
2. To fertilize; to supply with the nutriment of plants; as, to enrich land by manure.
3. To store; to supply with any thing splendid or valuable; as, to enrich the mind with knowledge.
ENRICHING, ppr. Making rich; fertilizing; supplying with valuable things.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 17:25

And the men of Israel said, Have ye seen this man that is come up? surely to defy Israel is he come up: and it shall be, that the man who killeth him, the king will enrich him with great riches, and will give him his daughter, and make his father's house free in Israel.
Ezekiel 27:33
When thy wares went forth out of the seas, thou filledst many people; thou didst enrich the kings of the earth with the multitude of thy riches and of thy merchandise.
2 Corinthians 9:11
Being enriched in every thing to all bountifulness, which causeth through us thanksgiving to God.
2 Corinthians 8:9
For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich.
corruption_summary: Enrichment is preached as the goal of faith, when Paul makes it a means to giving and Christ's own movement runs the other way.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity teaching takes texts like 2 Corinthians 9:11 and stops in the middle of the sentence. Paul writes being enriched in every thing to all bountifulness, and the preposition governs everything: the enriching has a stated destination, which is liberality, and a stated end, which is thanksgiving to God from the recipients. Take away the second half and the verse becomes a promise of personal accumulation, which is precisely the opposite of what the whole chapter is doing — Paul is raising famine relief for poor saints in Jerusalem, and the Macedonians he holds up as the model gave out of deep poverty and beyond their power.

The chapter before supplies the pattern that settles it: though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich. The enriching of the saints runs through the impoverishment of the Son, which makes a doctrine of Christian wealth-accumulation not merely mistaken but a reversal of the gospel it claims. Scripture is not embarrassed by wealth honestly held — Abraham, Job, Barzillai, Lydia — but it never treats it as the point. David is the fitting illustration: he was offered great riches for killing Goliath, and the reason he gave for going down to the brook was the honour of God's name.
roots_summary: Hebrew ashar, to be or make rich — 1 Samuel 17:25, Ezekiel 27:33; Greek ploutizo, to make wealthy — 2 Corinthians 9:11, 8:9; haplotes, liberality — the destination.
roots_lines: Hebrew ashar — to be rich, to make rich; 1 Samuel 17:25 and Proverbs 10:22.
Greek ploutizo — to make wealthy; 2 Corinthians 6:10, 8:9, 9:11 — every occurrence about giving.
Greek haplotes — singleness, and so liberality; the stated destination of the enriching.
Greek eucharistia — thanksgiving; the stated end of the whole transaction.
Greek ptocheuo — to become poor; 2 Corinthians 8:9, of Christ.
usage: “The king will enrich him with great riches” — and David spoke of the name of the LORD.
“Enriched in every thing to all bountifulness” — the preposition carries the doctrine.
“Though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor” — the movement of the gospel.

pos: v. (struck with terror; forbidden to soldiers before battle, to the church before its adversaries, and felt by the disciples in the presence of the risen Christ)
etymology: From Latin terrere, to frighten, through terrificare, to make afraid. The Hebrew at Deuteronomy 20:3 is arats, to tremble or be terrified; the Greek at Philippians 1:28 is pturo, to be startled — a word used of horses shying.
biblical_def: Twice the word appears in a prohibition, which is worth pausing over: God commands men not to be terrified. In the priest's address before battle: “Hear, O Israel, ye approach this day unto battle against your enemies: let not your hearts faint, fear not, and do not tremble, neither be ye terrified because of them” (Deuteronomy 20:3) — and the reason follows, that the LORD goeth with them to fight for them. Our Lord gives the same command about the end: “when ye shall hear of wars and commotions, be not terrified: for these things must first come to pass; but the end is not by and by” (Luke 21:9). Paul makes composure under opposition itself a sign: “And in nothing terrified by your adversaries: which is to them an evident token of perdition, but to you of salvation, and that of God” (Philippians 1:28). The Greek pturo is the word for a horse shying at a shadow, and Paul says the church's failure to shy is legible to its enemies. The fourth occurrence is honest about how hard the command is: when the risen Christ stood among them, “they were terrified and affrighted, and supposed that they had seen a spirit” (Luke 24:37).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines terrify as to frighten, to alarm or shock with fear — and notes it is a stronger word than merely to fear.
webster_full: TERRIFIED, pp. Frightened; affrighted.
TERRIFY, v.t. To frighten; to alarm or shock with fear.
When ye shall hear of wars, be not terrified. Luke 21.
TERRIBLE, a. Frightful; adapted to excite terror; dreadful; formidable.
TERROR, n. Extreme fear; violent dread; fright; fear that agitates the body and mind.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 20:3
And shall say unto them, Hear, O Israel, ye approach this day unto battle against your enemies: let not your hearts faint, fear not, and do not tremble, neither be ye terrified because of them;
Luke 21:9
But when ye shall hear of wars and commotions, be not terrified: for these things must first come to pass; but the end is not by and by.
Philippians 1:28
And in nothing terrified by your adversaries: which is to them an evident token of perdition, but to you of salvation, and that of God.
Luke 24:37
But they were terrified and affrighted, and supposed that they had seen a spirit.
corruption_summary: Fear is treated as involuntary and therefore beyond command, which makes the many biblical prohibitions of it unintelligible.
corruption_paragraphs: If fear is purely a physiological reflex, then be not terrified is as sensible as commanding a man not to sneeze, and the hundred-odd fear not sayings of Scripture become well-meant encouragement rather than commands. The Bible treats fear as genuinely commandable, and it does so by always attaching a ground. Deuteronomy 20 does not say be brave; it says the LORD your God goeth with you, to fight for you against your enemies, to save you. Luke 21 does not say the wars are trivial; it says these things must first come to pass — they are inside a plan. Fear is addressed at the level of what a man believes to be true, which is why the remedy is always a fact and never a technique.

Luke 24:37 keeps the doctrine honest. The eleven, hearing the very reports they had hoped for, saw Christ and were terrified — and He did not rebuke them for it as though terror were sin. He showed them His hands and His feet, invited them to handle Him, ate a piece of broiled fish before them, and opened their understanding that they might understand the scriptures. That is the pastoral pattern: the answer to fear is evidence and Scripture, patiently given. Philippians 1:28 states what such settled fearlessness eventually becomes — a token, legible to adversaries, that this salvation is of God.
roots_summary: Hebrew arats, to tremble, be terrified — Deuteronomy 20:3; Greek ptoeo, to be startled — Luke 21:9, 24:37; pturo, to shy as a frightened horse — Philippians 1:28.
roots_lines: Hebrew arats — to tremble, dread, be terrified; Deuteronomy 20:3 and Joshua 1:9.
Greek ptoeo — to be startled or terrified; Luke 21:9 and Luke 24:37.
Greek pturo — to be frightened as a horse shying; Philippians 1:28, its only New Testament occurrence.
Greek endeixis — an evident token or proof; what the church's composure becomes.
Latin terrere, to frighten — the source of the English word.
usage: “Neither be ye terrified because of them” — a command, with a reason attached.
“In nothing terrified by your adversaries” — composure legible as a token.
“They were terrified and affrighted” — and He showed them His hands and His feet.

pos: v. and n. (to desire; the word of Paul's unthinkable prayer for Israel, of the prosperity of the wicked, and of John's greeting to Gaius)
etymology: From Old English wyscan, to desire. The Greek at Romans 9:3 is euchomai, to pray or vow — a much stronger word than English wish; at 3 John 2 the same verb governs a greeting.
biblical_def: The English word is weak and the Greek behind it is not. Euchomai means to pray or to vow, and Paul uses it for the most extreme statement in his writings: “For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Romans 9:3). He has just finished Romans 8, which ends with nothing being able to separate him from the love of God in Christ, and he opens Romans 9 by saying he could pray to be accursed — anathema — if it would save Israel. The imperfect tense marks it as a wish he knows cannot be granted; Moses had made the same offer, blot me out of thy book. Asaph uses the word of what the wicked appear to have: “Their eyes stand out with fatness: they have more than heart could wish” (Psalm 73:7), in the psalm whose whole argument is that this appearance held until he went into the sanctuary. Paul uses it for the church's maturity, “this also we wish, even your perfection” (2 Corinthians 13:9), and John for a friend: “Beloved, I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth” (3 John 2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wish as to have a desire or strong desire, either for what is or is not supposed to be obtainable.
webster_full: WISH, v.i. To have a desire or strong desire, either for what is or is not supposed to be obtainable.
It usually expresses less than long and covet.
2. To be disposed or inclined to.
WISH, v.t. To desire; to long for; to have a strong desire for.
WISH, n. Desire; sometimes eager desire; longing.
scriptures: Romans 9:3
For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh:
Psalm 73:7
Their eyes stand out with fatness: they have more than heart could wish.
2 Corinthians 13:9
For we are glad, when we are weak, and ye are strong: and this also we wish, even your perfection.
3 John 1:2
Beloved, I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth.
corruption_summary: 3 John 2 has been made the charter text of the health-and-wealth message, though it is an ordinary letter greeting with a spiritual measure built into it.
corruption_paragraphs: “I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health” is quoted more often than almost any verse in the prosperity movement, and two facts about it are usually withheld. First, the form is the standard health-wish of an ancient letter — the Greek equivalent of I hope this finds you well — and it is John's greeting to one man, Gaius, not a promise to the church. Second, and decisively, it contains its own measure: even as thy soul prospereth. John wishes Gaius bodily prosperity in exact proportion to the state of his soul, which he has just learned is excellent because brethren testified of the truth that was in him. Applied generally, that clause would ruin most of the sermons preached from it.

Romans 9:3 is the passage that shows what Christian desire looks like when it is fully formed, and it runs the other way entirely. Paul, having just declared himself inseparable from Christ, says he could pray to be anathema for his kinsmen. Whether such a wish could be lawful is a question the commentators have long debated; what is beyond debate is what it reveals. The apostle who wrote the most rigorous statement of election in Scripture wrote it out of great heaviness and continual sorrow of heart for those not saved. Any doctrine of election held without that sorrow has been learned from somewhere other than Paul.
roots_summary: Greek euchomai, to pray or vow — Romans 9:3, 3 John 2, 2 Corinthians 13:9; anathema, accursed — Romans 9:3; Hebrew maskith leb, the imagination of the heart — Psalm 73:7.
roots_lines: Greek euchomai — to pray, to vow; far stronger than English wish; Romans 9:3 and 3 John 2.
Greek anathema — devoted to destruction, accursed; what Paul says he could pray to become.
Greek euodoo — to have a prosperous journey, to prosper; 3 John 2, twice in one verse.
Greek katartisis — perfecting, restoration to order; 2 Corinthians 13:9.
Old English wyscan — to desire; the source of the English word.
usage: “I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ” — the Greek is I could pray.
“Even as thy soul prospereth” — the measure built into the greeting.
“They have more than heart could wish” — until Asaph went into the sanctuary.

pos: n. (an occurrence without apparent cause; used by the Philistine diviners as a hypothesis, by the Preacher as an observation, and by our Lord in a parable — never by Scripture as an explanation)
etymology: From Latin cadere, to fall, through Old French cheance, a falling out — the same root as cadence and accident. The Hebrew at 1 Samuel 6:9 is miqreh, a happening, from qarah, to befall; the Greek at Luke 10:31 is sugkuria, a coincidence.
biblical_def: Scripture uses the word, and never as an ultimate account of anything. The Philistine priests devise a test for the ark and state the alternatives exactly: if the kine go up to Bethshemesh, the LORD did this; “but if not, then we shall know that it is not his hand that smote us: it was a chance that happened to us” (1 Samuel 6:9). The kine went straight up, lowing as they went, turning aside neither to the right hand nor to the left — and chance was excluded by an experiment the pagans designed themselves. The Preacher observes what appears from below: “the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong… but time and chance happeneth to them all” (Ecclesiastes 9:11) — the phrase under the sun governs the whole book, and it describes the view from ground level, not the truth about heaven. Our Lord says “by chance there came down a certain priest that way” (Luke 10:31), using the ordinary human idiom in a parable to mean the priest had no plan to be there. And a young Amalekite says he happened by chance on mount Gilboa (2 Samuel 1:6) — in a speech Scripture shows to be a lie.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines chance as an event that happens without being designed or expected, and observes that in reality there is no such thing, since every event has a cause.
webster_full: CHANCE, n. An event that happens, falls out or takes place, without being contrived, intended, expected or foreseen; the effect of an unknown cause, or the unusual or unexpected effect of a known cause; accident; casualty; fortuitous event.
In strictness of speech, chance has no existence; there is no such thing as an event without a cause.
2. Fortune; what fortune may bring; as, they must take their chance.
3. An event, good or evil; success or misfortune; luck.
CHANCE, v.i. To happen; to fall out; to come or arrive without design or expectation.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 6:9

And see, if it goeth up by the way of his own coast to Bethshemesh, then he hath done us this great evil: but if not, then we shall know that it is not his hand that smote us: it was a chance that happened to us.
Ecclesiastes 9:11

I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all.
Luke 10:31
And by chance there came down a certain priest that way: and when he saw him, he passed by on the other side.
Proverbs 16:33
The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Chance has been promoted from a description of human ignorance into a metaphysical cause — a thing that explains outcomes rather than confessing that we do not know them.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster saw the point clearly in 1828: in strictness of speech, chance has no existence; there is no such thing as an event without a cause. The word properly names a limit in the observer, not a power in the world. Modern usage has quietly made it a cause — things happen by chance, and the phrase is offered as an explanation that closes the question. It explains nothing. To say an event occurred by chance is to say one does not know why it occurred, which is often a perfectly honest thing to say and is never a rival account to providence. The Reformed doctrine does not deny contingency as men experience it; it denies that contingency is ultimate.

Proverbs 16:33 is the decisive text and it is deliberately provocative: the lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD. The lot was the ancient world's purest instance of randomness, and Scripture assigns its outcome entirely to God — which is why the lot fell on Jonah, why the land was divided by lot, and why Matthias was chosen by it. Ecclesiastes 9:11 is not a contradiction but a report from under the sun: from ground level the swift lose races and the wise go hungry, and no pattern is visible. Both are true. The believer lives with the second and rests in the first.
roots_summary: Hebrew miqreh, a happening — 1 Samuel 6:9, Ecclesiastes 9:11; qarah, to befall; Greek sugkuria, coincidence — Luke 10:31; goral, a lot — Proverbs 16:33.
roots_lines: Hebrew miqreh — an occurrence, a happening; 1 Samuel 6:9 and Ecclesiastes 9:11.
Hebrew qarah — to befall, to meet; the root of miqreh.
Hebrew goral — a lot; Proverbs 16:33, whose disposing is of the LORD.
Greek sugkuria — a coincidence, a chance meeting; Luke 10:31, its only New Testament occurrence.
Latin cadere, to fall — the root of chance, cadence, and accident.
usage: “It was a chance that happened to us” — a hypothesis the Philistines tested and disproved.
“Time and chance happeneth to them all” — the view under the sun.
“The whole disposing thereof is of the LORD” — of the lot, the purest randomness known.

pos: a. (of the earth, made of dust; Paul's word in 1 Corinthians 15 for the first Adam and for all who bear his image)
etymology: From earth — Old English eorthe — with -y. The Greek is choikos, made of dust or loose soil, from chous, poured-out earth — a word Paul appears to coin from the Septuagint of Genesis 2:7, where God formed man of the dust of the ground.
biblical_def: The word occurs three times, all within three verses of the great resurrection chapter, and it carries a whole anthropology. “The first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:47). Paul's choikos reaches back to Genesis 2:7 — the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground — and sets against it the second man, who is not a second creation out of dust but the Lord from heaven. The consequence for humanity is stated: “As is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy: and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15:48). Two families, two heads, two natures inherited. And then the promise: “And as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15:49). This is federal headship stated as plainly as anywhere in Scripture, and it is the same doctrine as Romans 5 — in Adam all die, in Christ shall all be made alive. Verse 45 names them: “The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit” (1 Corinthians 15:45).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines earthy as consisting of earth, resembling earth, and figuratively gross or not refined — citing the Corinthians text.
webster_full: EARTHY, a. Consisting of earth; as earthy matter.
2. Resembling earth; as an earthy taste or smell.
3. Partaking of earth; terrene.
The first man is of the earth, earthy. 1 Cor. 15.
4. Inhabiting the earth; terrestrial. 5. Relating to earth; gross; not refined; unrefined.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 15:47
The first man is of the earth, earthy: the second man is the Lord from heaven.
1 Corinthians 15:48
As is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy: and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly.
1 Corinthians 15:49
And as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.
1 Corinthians 15:45
And so it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a quickening spirit.
corruption_summary: Deny a historical Adam and the whole argument collapses, since Paul's case for the resurrection body rests on two literal men and two real headships.
corruption_paragraphs: The standard accommodation to evolutionary anthropology is that Adam is a literary or representative figure rather than the first man, and that Paul's use of him is an argument from a shared cultural story. 1 Corinthians 15 makes that reading impossible without dismantling the chapter. Paul's argument for the nature of the resurrection body runs entirely on the parallel between two men: the first man of the earth, the second man from heaven; the image of the earthy borne now, the image of the heavenly borne then. If the first term of the parallel is a figure, the second is not secured by it. Romans 5 has the same structure — by one man sin entered, by one man came the resurrection of the dead — and Luke 3 traces the genealogy of Christ to Adam without any change of register.

The word earthy also guards against the opposite ancient error. Paul is not saying that matter is base and spirit is fine; that is Gnosticism, and it is refuted by the very doctrine he is teaching, since the resurrection is a bodily resurrection. He is saying that the body we now bear derives from a man made of dust and shares his mortality, and that the body we shall bear derives from the last Adam who is a quickening spirit. It is sown in corruption and raised in incorruption — the same body, transformed, not exchanged for a bodiless state. Christianity is not the escape of the soul from the earthy; it is the redemption of the earthy.
roots_summary: Greek choikos, made of dust — 1 Corinthians 15:47-49; chous, poured-out earth; epouranios, heavenly — the contrast; Hebrew aphar, dust — Genesis 2:7.
roots_lines: Greek choikos — made of dust or loose earth; only in 1 Corinthians 15:47-49.
Greek chous — poured earth, dust; the Septuagint word at Genesis 2:7.
Greek epouranios — heavenly; the answering adjective for the second man.
Greek zoopoieo — to make alive, quicken; the last Adam as a quickening spirit.
Hebrew aphar — dust of the ground; Genesis 2:7, the source of Paul's figure.
usage: “The first man is of the earth, earthy” — a straight quotation of Genesis 2:7.
“As is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy” — two heads, two families.
“We shall also bear the image of the heavenly” — the body redeemed, not discarded.
